provisions.sourceLine: s 3B(1)(a), (b), (f)-(g); s 3B(2)(a)  Civil liability excluded from Act
provisions.oneLine: Check the listed exclusions before applying the Civil Liability Act.
provisions.plain: The Act does not govern every civil claim. The listed parts of s 3B exclude or partly exclude intentional injury, sexual misconduct, specified dust-disease and workers-compensation liabilities. The exclusions contain important carve-backs. The listed s 3B(2)(a) also tells you which negligence divisions apply to motor accidents. Start with the type of liability and identify which Part remains available.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A worker sues for a workplace injury. You cannot start by applying every CLA negligence provision: first identify whether the workers-compensation exclusion governs this particular award. A sexual-abuse claim likewise needs the Part 1B carve-back considered.
conditions: Apply only the law-list scope: s 3B(1)(a), (b), (f)–(g), and s 3B(2)(a).
Paragraph (1)(a) requires an intentional act done with intent to cause injury/death, or sexual assault/other sexual misconduct; intentional conduct alone is not the stated test.
Paragraph (1)(b) concerns proceedings of the kind referred to by s 11 of the Dust Diseases Tribunal Act 1989.

Paragraph (1)(f) concerns an award within Division 3 of Part 5 of the Workers Compensation Act 1987. Paragraph (1)(g) excludes civil liability for compensation under the Workers Compensation Act 1987, Workers Compensation (Bush Fire, Emergency and Rescue Services) Act 1987, Workers’ Compensation (Dust Diseases) Act 1942 and Anti-Discrimination Act 1977, or a benefit payable under the Sporting Injuries Insurance Act 1978.
exceptions: Paragraph (1)(a) retains Part 1B; s 15B; s 18(1) only in its application to damages for loss within s 18(1)(c); Part 7 only for the specified intentional injury/death liability; and Part 2A.
Paragraph (1)(b) retains ss 15A and 15B, and s 18(1) only in its application to damages for loss within s 18(1)(c).
Paragraph (1)(f) excepts Part 1B from its whole-Act exclusion.
Section 3B(2)(a) applies Divisions 1–4 and 8 of Part 1A to motor accidents.
limits: The full section contains other exclusions; those are not silently added to this examinable entry.
The explanatory note accompanying paragraph (f) is retained separately in sourceNotes and is not part of the Act.
provisions.examUse: Use at the application stage before selecting a CLA test or defence.
pitfalls: Do not say all deliberate acts are excluded.
Do not erase the express carve-backs.
Do not expand this filter to every subsection of s 3B.
provisions.text:

(a) civil liability of a person in respect of an intentional act that is done by the person
         with intent to cause injury or death or that is sexual assault or other sexual
         misconduct committed by the person—the whole Act except—

          (ia) Part 1B (Child abuse—liability of organisations), and

          (i) section 15B and section 18(1) (in its application to damages for any loss of the

provisions.sourceLine: s 3C  Act operates to exclude or limit vicarious liability
provisions.oneLine: A CLA exclusion or limit on the tortfeasor also reaches another person’s vicarious liability for that tort.
provisions.plain: If the CLA removes or limits the civil liability of the person who committed a tort, the same statutory protection also operates on a person sued vicariously for that tort. This provision concerns the effect of an existing exclusion or limit; it does not itself decide whether an employment relationship or another basis for vicarious liability exists.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: An employer is sued for an employee’s tort. If an applicable CLA provision limits liability for that tort, s 3C carries that limit to the employer’s vicarious liability. You still have to establish why the employer is vicariously liable.
conditions: Identify a provision of the CLA that excludes or limits civil liability for a tort.
Identify the other person’s vicarious liability for the same tort.
limits: This is not a general immunity for employers.
It does not establish an employment relationship or course-of-employment connection.
provisions.examUse: Apply after identifying both the underlying tort and the basis of vicarious liability.
pitfalls: Do not use s 3C to create vicarious liability.
provisions.text:
Any provision of this Act that excludes or limits the civil liability of a person for a tort also
operates to exclude or limit the vicarious liability of another person for that tort.

provisions.sourceLine: s 5  Definitions
provisions.oneLine: Part 1A defines harm broadly and negligence as a failure to use reasonable care and skill.
provisions.plain: For the negligence Part, harm includes injury or death, property damage and economic loss. Personal injury includes prenatal injury, impairment of a physical or mental condition, and disease. These definitions explain why the statutory negligence framework can apply to economic loss as well as physical accidents; they do not prove that a duty is owed in every such situation.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A careless valuation causes only a financial loss. That loss can still be harm under Part 1A. The claimant must separately establish the special duty requirements for pure economic loss and all the remaining elements.
conditions: These definitions operate in Part 1A.
Harm includes personal injury/death, property damage and economic loss.
Negligence means failure to exercise reasonable care and skill.
Personal injury includes prenatal injury, physical/mental impairment and disease.
limits: A definition of harm is not an automatic right to recover.
provisions.examUse: Classify the damage before addressing duty, breach, causation and defences.
pitfalls: Do not exclude pure economic loss merely because no person or property was physically hurt.
provisions.text:
In this Part—

harm means harm of any kind, including the following—

(a) personal injury or death,

(b) damage to property,

(c) economic loss.

negligence means failure to exercise reasonable care and skill.

personal injury includes—

(a) pre-natal injury, and

(b) impairment of a person’s physical or mental condition, and

(c) disease.

provisions.sourceLine: s 5A  Application of Part
provisions.oneLine: Part 1A follows negligent conduct, regardless of the legal form of the damages claim.
provisions.plain: A damages claim for harm resulting from negligence falls within Part 1A even if the claimant pleads contract, statute or another cause of action rather than tort. However, liabilities excluded by s 3B remain excluded. The section prevents a change of pleading label from bypassing the negligence Part.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A customer frames a careless-service claim as a broken contractual promise. If the harm resulted from a failure to exercise reasonable care and skill, Part 1A can still apply, subject to its exclusions.
conditions: A claim for damages.
Harm resulting from negligence.
The cause of action may be tort, contract, statute or otherwise.
exceptions: Civil liability excluded from Part 1A by s 3B is not covered.
limits: Part 1A provisions still have their own wording and requirements.
provisions.examUse: Establish statutory application near the beginning of a negligence answer.
pitfalls: Do not assume pleading contract avoids the CLA.
Do not skip s 3B.
provisions.text:
(1) This Part applies to any claim for damages for harm resulting from negligence,
    regardless of whether the claim is brought in tort, in contract, under statute or
    otherwise.

(2) This Part does not apply to civil liability that is excluded from the operation of this Part
    by section 3B.

provisions.sourceLine: s 5B  General principles
provisions.oneLine: Breach requires a foreseeable, not insignificant risk and precautions a reasonable person would take.
provisions.plain: The court asks prospectively what a reasonable person in the defendant’s position would have done about the identified risk. The risk must be foreseeable and not insignificant. The reasonableness of precautions involves probability, seriousness, the burden of precautions and social utility, together with any other relevant matters. A bad outcome alone does not prove breach.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: For an unfenced drop near a busy path, identify the risk of someone falling. Then weigh how likely a fall was, how serious it could be, the cost and practicability of fencing, and the activity’s utility. The presence of injury does not replace this analysis.
conditions: The risk was known or ought to have been known.
The risk was not insignificant.
A reasonable person in the defendant’s position would have taken the proposed precautions.
Consider probability, likely seriousness, burden of precautions and social utility, among other relevant matters.
limits: This provision addresses failure to take precautions, not the whole existence of a duty.
The statutory expression is not insignificant; do not substitute the common-law not far-fetched or fanciful threshold.
provisions.examUse: State the precise risk and precaution, then apply each statutory consideration to the facts.
pitfalls: Do not reason backwards from the accident.
Do not merely list the four factors without weighing them.
provisions.text:
(1) A person is not negligent in failing to take precautions against a risk of harm unless—

     (a) the risk was foreseeable (that is, it is a risk of which the person knew or ought to
         have known), and

     (b) the risk was not insignificant, and

     (c) in the circumstances, a reasonable person in the person’s position would have
         taken those precautions.

(2) In determining whether a reasonable person would have taken precautions against a
    risk of harm, the court is to consider the following (amongst other relevant things)—

     (a) the probability that the harm would occur if care were not taken,

     (b) the likely seriousness of the harm,

     (c) the burden of taking precautions to avoid the risk of harm,

     (d) the social utility of the activity that creates the risk of harm.

provisions.sourceLine: s 5C  Other principles
provisions.oneLine: Breach analysis counts similar risks and avoids treating alternatives or repairs as automatic admissions.
provisions.plain: When assessing the burden of precautions, consider comparable risks for which the defendant is responsible, not just one isolated danger. Showing that an activity could have been done differently does not itself establish liability. Nor does later remedial work itself establish liability or admit it.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A council repairs one pavement after an accident. The repair alone does not prove the earlier condition was negligent. A proposed inspection programme must also be assessed across the similar risks for which the council is responsible.
conditions: Include the burden of precautions against similar risks.
An alternative way of doing the activity does not itself establish or affect liability.
Later preventive action does not itself establish or affect liability or constitute an admission.
limits: The words of itself matter: relevant surrounding evidence is not made irrelevant by this provision.
provisions.examUse: Use while applying the burden factor and when the facts mention subsequent repairs or alternative methods.
pitfalls: Do not infer breach solely from a later repair.
Do not assess a system-wide precaution as if only one location existed.
provisions.text:
In proceedings relating to liability for negligence—

(a) the burden of taking precautions to avoid a risk of harm includes the burden of taking
    precautions to avoid similar risks of harm for which the person may be responsible,
    and

(b) the fact that a risk of harm could have been avoided by doing something in a different
    way does not of itself give rise to or affect liability for the way in which the thing was
    done, and

(c) the subsequent taking of action that would (had the action been taken earlier) have
    avoided a risk of harm does not of itself give rise to or affect liability in respect of the
    risk and does not of itself constitute an admission of liability in connection with the
    risk.

provisions.sourceLine: s 5D  General principles
provisions.oneLine: Separate factual causation from the appropriate scope of responsibility for the harm.
provisions.plain: First ask whether the negligence was a necessary condition of the particular harm. Then ask whether the defendant should legally be responsible for that harm. Exceptional cases where the necessary-condition test cannot be established require established principles and a reasoned responsibility analysis. If the claimant’s hypothetical choice matters, assess it subjectively from all relevant circumstances, subject to the restriction on self-serving statements made after the harm.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: If a doctor omitted a warning, ask what this patient would have done if properly warned, and whether avoiding that choice would have prevented the harm. Even if factual causation is established, separately ask whether the harm falls within the responsibility attached to the warning duty.
conditions: Factual causation: negligence was a necessary condition of the occurrence of the harm.
Scope: it is appropriate for liability to extend to that harm.
Exceptional factual-causation cases are assessed in accordance with established principles and the responsibility question.
A claimant’s hypothetical conduct is assessed subjectively in all relevant circumstances.
exceptions: A claimant’s statement made after the harm about what they would have done is inadmissible except to the extent it is against their interest.
limits: The exceptional-case provision does not dispense generally with proof of causation.
Section 5D(4) separately requires the responsibility question for scope.
provisions.examUse: Use separate headings for s 5D(1)(a) and (b), and explain any reliance on (2), (3) or (4).
pitfalls: Do not merge breach, factual causation and scope.
Do not treat a claimant’s later assertion as conclusive proof.
provisions.text:
(1) A determination that negligence caused particular harm comprises the following
    elements—

     (a) that the negligence was a necessary condition of the occurrence of the harm
         (factual causation), and

     (b) that it is appropriate for the scope of the negligent person’s liability to extend to
         the harm so caused (scope of liability).

(2) In determining in an exceptional case, in accordance with established principles,
    whether negligence that cannot be established as a necessary condition of the
    occurrence of harm should be accepted as establishing factual causation, the court is
    to consider (amongst other relevant things) whether or not and why responsibility for
    the harm should be imposed on the negligent party.

(3) If it is relevant to the determination of factual causation to determine what the person
    who suffered harm would have done if the negligent person had not been negligent—

     (a) the matter is to be determined subjectively in the light of all relevant
         circumstances, subject to paragraph (b), and

     (b) any statement made by the person after suffering the harm about what he or she

          would have done is inadmissible except to the extent (if any) that the statement is
          against his or her interest.

(4) For the purpose of determining the scope of liability, the court is to consider (amongst
    other relevant things) whether or not and why responsibility for the harm should be
    imposed on the negligent party.

provisions.sourceLine: s 5E  Onus of proof
provisions.oneLine: The claimant bears the balance-of-probabilities burden on every fact relevant to causation.
provisions.plain: For negligence causation, the plaintiff must establish relevant facts as more probable than not. A defendant does not have to disprove causation merely because breach has been shown. Inferences can be important, but must satisfy the civil burden.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A shop failed to clean a spill. The plaintiff still has to prove, using the evidence and permissible inferences, that a reasonable cleaning system would probably have prevented this slip.
conditions: Proceedings relate to liability for negligence.
The plaintiff bears the onus for any fact relevant to causation.
The standard is the balance of probabilities.
limits: Breach does not itself reverse this onus.
provisions.examUse: State the onus when analysing uncertain counterfactuals, timing or competing causes.
pitfalls: Do not say the defendant must prove its negligence made no difference.
provisions.text:
In proceedings relating to liability for negligence, the plaintiff always bears the onus of
proving, on the balance of probabilities, any fact relevant to the issue of causation.

provisions.sourceLine: s 5F  Meaning of “obvious risk”
provisions.oneLine: An obvious risk is judged from the reasonable person in the claimant’s position, even if unlikely or hidden.
provisions.plain: Obviousness is an objective inquiry about the risk in its circumstances. A risk may be obvious because it is patent or common knowledge. A low chance of occurrence does not prevent obviousness, and the danger or its physical cause need not be conspicuous or observable.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: An ordinary person may appreciate the risk of striking a shallow riverbed when diving, even without seeing the bottom. The question remains what risk was obvious to a reasonable person in this claimant’s position in these circumstances.
conditions: Identify the relevant risk at an appropriate level of specificity.
Ask whether it would have been obvious to a reasonable person in the claimant’s position.
Patent risks and common-knowledge risks are included.
limits: A low-probability risk can be obvious.
The risk or its source need not be prominent, conspicuous or physically observable.
This definition is not itself a complete defence to every negligence allegation.
provisions.examUse: Use before ss 5G, 5H or 5L, identifying the specific risk that materialised.
pitfalls: Do not equate obvious with likely.
Do not treat all risks of an activity as interchangeable.
provisions.text:
(1) For the purposes of this Division, an obvious risk to a person who suffers harm is a
    risk that, in the circumstances, would have been obvious to a reasonable person in the
    position of that person.

(2) Obvious risks include risks that are patent or a matter of common knowledge.

(3) A risk of something occurring can be an obvious risk even though it has a low
    probability of occurring.

(4) A risk can be an obvious risk even if the risk (or a condition or circumstance that gives
    rise to the risk) is not prominent, conspicuous or physically observable.

provisions.sourceLine: s 5G  Injured persons presumed to be aware of obvious risks
provisions.oneLine: The claimant is presumed to know an obvious risk unless they prove otherwise.
provisions.plain: Where the harm arose from an obvious risk, awareness is presumed in negligence proceedings. The claimant can rebut that presumption on the balance of probabilities. Awareness of the type of risk is sufficient; knowledge of its precise extent or mechanism is unnecessary.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A diver may know the general type of danger of hitting submerged ground without knowing the precise depth or the particular injury that will follow. The awareness presumption can still operate, although it remains rebuttable.
conditions: An obvious risk under s 5F.
Negligence proceedings relating to the claimant’s harm.
Knowledge of the type or kind of risk suffices.
exceptions: The claimant may prove on the balance of probabilities that they were not aware of the risk.
limits: Presumed knowledge is not the same as voluntary acceptance of legal responsibility.
provisions.examUse: Analyse awareness separately from any legal defence requiring acceptance of the risk.
pitfalls: Do not turn a rebuttable awareness presumption into automatic consent to the defendant’s negligence.
provisions.text:
(1) In proceedings relating to liability for negligence, a person who suffers harm is
    presumed to have been aware of the risk of harm if it was an obvious risk, unless the
    person proves on the balance of probabilities that he or she was not aware of the risk.

(2) For the purposes of this section, a person is aware of a risk if the person is aware of
    the type or kind of risk, even if the person is not aware of the precise nature, extent or
    manner of occurrence of the risk.

provisions.sourceLine: s 5H  No proactive duty to warn of obvious risk
provisions.oneLine: There is ordinarily no proactive duty to warn of an obvious risk, subject to three specified exceptions.
provisions.plain: A defendant ordinarily need not warn another person about an obvious risk. The rule does not apply where the claimant requested advice about the risk, a written law requires a warning, or a professional service involves a risk of the claimant’s death or personal injury. Removing this statutory protection does not itself establish that a duty to warn exists.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A patient asks a surgeon about a procedure’s risks. The surgeon cannot simply rely on the no-warning rule for obvious risks: the request and the professional-service exception must be considered. The applicable warning duty still needs analysis.
conditions: The alleged duty is a duty to warn.
The risk is obvious to the claimant under s 5F.
exceptions: The claimant requested advice or information about the risk.
A written law requires a warning.
The defendant is a professional and the risk concerns the claimant’s death or personal injury from the professional service.
limits: Subsection (2) does not presume a duty to warn in any of the exceptions.
The section does not erase other possible duties to take precautions.
provisions.examUse: Separate failure to warn from failure to make premises or an activity reasonably safe.
pitfalls: Do not infer no duty of care of any kind.
Do not infer a warning duty automatically from an exception.
provisions.text:
(1) A person (the defendant) does not owe a duty of care to another person (the
    plaintiff) to warn of an obvious risk to the plaintiff.

(2) This section does not apply if—

     (a) the plaintiff has requested advice or information about the risk from the
         defendant, or

     (b) the defendant is required by a written law to warn the plaintiff of the risk, or

     (c) the defendant is a professional and the risk is a risk of the death of or personal
         injury to the plaintiff from the provision of a professional service by the defendant.

(3) Subsection (2) does not give rise to a presumption of a duty to warn of a risk in the
    circumstances referred to in that subsection.

provisions.sourceLine: s 5I  No liability for materialisation of inherent risk
provisions.oneLine: An unavoidable inherent risk can exclude negligence liability, but not a distinct duty to warn.
provisions.plain: An inherent risk is one that reasonable care and skill cannot avoid. If that risk materialises, negligence liability is excluded for the resulting harm. A danger that was simply not avoided is not necessarily inherent. The statute preserves any liability connected with a duty to warn.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A treatment complication may occur even with reasonable skill. That can raise s 5I for the occurrence of the complication. If there should have been a warning about the complication, that warning question remains separate.
conditions: The harm resulted from materialisation of the identified risk.
The risk could not be avoided by reasonable care and skill.
exceptions: The section does not exclude liability connected with a duty to warn of the risk.
limits: Inherent does not mean merely usual, obvious, or statistically possible.
provisions.examUse: Test whether reasonable care could have avoided the risk, then preserve any warning issue.
pitfalls: Do not confuse unavoidable risk with avoidable careless performance.
provisions.text:
(1) A person is not liable in negligence for harm suffered by another person as a result of
    the materialisation of an inherent risk.

(2) An inherent risk is a risk of something occurring that cannot be avoided by the
    exercise of reasonable care and skill.

(3) This section does not operate to exclude liability in connection with a duty to warn of
    a risk.

provisions.sourceLine: s 5K  Definitions
provisions.oneLine: The recreational defence definitions include leisure broadly but require significant physical risk for dangerous activities.
provisions.plain: Recreational activity includes sport, leisure pursuits, and activities at places where people ordinarily engage in sport or leisure. A dangerous recreational activity is one involving a significant risk of physical harm. Obvious risk uses the Division 4 meaning. The activity’s actual character and the relevant risk must still be examined.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A person playing an informal sport can be engaged in a recreational activity even without an organised competition. Whether it is dangerous requires a separate assessment of significant physical risk; the label sport does not settle it.
conditions: Dangerous recreational activity: recreational activity involving a significant risk of physical harm.
Recreational activity includes organised or unorganised sport, enjoyment/relaxation/leisure pursuits, and relevant activities at ordinary recreation places.
Obvious risk has the Division 4 meaning.
limits: Recreational and dangerous recreational are different thresholds.
provisions.examUse: Define the activity before applying s 5L or a recreational risk warning.
pitfalls: Do not assume every recreational activity is dangerous.
provisions.text:
In this Division—

dangerous recreational activity means a recreational activity that involves a
significant risk of physical harm.

obvious risk has the same meaning as it has in Division 4.

recreational activity includes—

(a) any sport (whether or not the sport is an organised activity), and

(b) any pursuit or activity engaged in for enjoyment, relaxation or leisure, and

(c) any pursuit or activity engaged in at a place (such as a beach, park or other public
    open space) where people ordinarily engage in sport or in any pursuit or activity for
    enjoyment, relaxation or leisure.

provisions.sourceLine: s 5L  No liability for harm suffered from obvious risks of dangerous recreational activities
provisions.oneLine: An obvious risk of a dangerous recreational activity can exclude liability even without the claimant’s actual awareness.
provisions.plain: The defendant is not liable in negligence for harm from the materialisation of an obvious risk of a dangerous recreational activity undertaken by the claimant. Both the activity and the risk need to be identified with care. Actual knowledge of the risk by this claimant is not required.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A rider is injured during a high-risk recreational event. Decide whether the event was a dangerous recreational activity and whether the actual injury arose from an obvious risk of that activity. A general statement that riding is risky is not enough.
conditions: The claimant engaged in a dangerous recreational activity under s 5K.
The relevant risk was obvious under s 5F.
The harm resulted from materialisation of that risk.
limits: Actual awareness is immaterial under subsection (2).
The actual risk must be matched to the risk that caused the harm.
provisions.examUse: Work through activity, dangerousness, obviousness and materialisation separately.
pitfalls: Do not use the claimant’s lack of subjective awareness as a complete answer.
Do not characterise the risk so broadly that the actual negligent danger disappears.
provisions.text:
(1) A person (the defendant) is not liable in negligence for harm suffered by another
    person (the plaintiff) as a result of the materialisation of an obvious risk of a

     dangerous recreational activity engaged in by the plaintiff.

(2) This section applies whether or not the plaintiff was aware of the risk.

provisions.sourceLine: s 5M  No duty of care for recreational activity where risk warning
provisions.oneLine: A qualifying recreational risk warning can remove a duty, but its many statutory limits matter.
provisions.plain: A warning can remove a duty to take care regarding a recreational risk if it is likely to warn people before they undertake the activity. It can be spoken, written or general, and actual receipt or understanding need not be proved. However, there are special rules for incapable people and limits involving the warning’s source, safety legislation, contradictory assurances and compulsory participation.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A climbing operator displays a warning but then expressly tells a customer that the warned-of danger cannot occur. The contradiction can prevent reliance on the warning to that extent. A young child also requires the special recipient rules to be checked.
conditions: A recreational activity and the particular risk are identified.
The warning is given in a way reasonably likely to warn people before participation.
A general warning must cover the general nature of the relevant risk.
The warning is by/on behalf of the defendant or the occupier.

For an incapable person, subsection (2)(a) requires control or accompaniment by a person who is neither incapable nor the defendant, and a warning to that other person; alternatively, (2)(b) permits a warning to a parent whether or not the parent controls or accompanies the person.
An incapable person lacks capacity to understand the warning because of young age or physical or mental disability. A parent is a person with parental responsibility who is not an incapable person.
The warning may be oral or written, including a sign.
exceptions: No reliance if it is established on the balance of probabilities that the harm resulted from contravention of a State or Commonwealth written-law provision establishing specific practices or procedures for personal safety.
No reliance to the extent the warning was contradicted by the defendant’s risk representation.
No reliance if the defendant required the claimant to undertake the activity.
limits: Actual receipt, understanding or capacity to understand need not be proved under subsection (3).
A warning does not itself prove that a risk is non-obvious/non-inherent or create a duty to take precautions.
The section preserves the effect of warnings for non-recreational activities.
provisions.examUse: Treat this as a multi-step statutory warning analysis, not a sign-equals-immunity shortcut.
pitfalls: Do not omit subsections (2), (6)–(9) and (12).
Do not confuse a risk warning with a contractual waiver.
provisions.text:
(1) A person (the defendant) does not owe a duty of care to another person who
    engages in a recreational activity (the plaintiff) to take care in respect of a risk of the
    activity if the risk was the subject of a risk warning to the plaintiff.

(2) If the person who suffers harm is an incapable person, the defendant may rely on a
    risk warning only if—

     (a) the incapable person was under the control of or accompanied by another person
         (who is not an incapable person and not the defendant) and the risk was the
         subject of a risk warning to that other person, or

     (b) the risk was the subject of a risk warning to a parent of the incapable person
         (whether or not the incapable person was under the control of or accompanied by
         the parent).

(3) For the purposes of subsections (1) and (2), a risk warning to a person in relation to a
    recreational activity is a warning that is given in a manner that is reasonably likely to
    result in people being warned of the risk before engaging in the recreational activity.
    The defendant is not required to establish that the person received or understood the
    warning or was capable of receiving or understanding the warning.

(4) A risk warning can be given orally or in writing (including by means of a sign or
    otherwise).

(5) A risk warning need not be specific to the particular risk and can be a general warning
    of risks that include the particular risk concerned (so long as the risk warning warns of
    the general nature of the particular risk).

(6) A defendant is not entitled to rely on a risk warning unless it is given by or on behalf
    of the defendant or by or on behalf of the occupier of the place where the recreational
    activity is engaged in.

(7) A defendant is not entitled to rely on a risk warning if it is established (on the balance
    of probabilities) that the harm concerned resulted from a contravention of a provision
    of a written law of the State or Commonwealth that establishes specific practices or
    procedures for the protection of personal safety.

(8) A defendant is not entitled to rely on a risk warning to a person to the extent that the
    warning was contradicted by any representation as to risk made by or on behalf of the
    defendant to the person.

(9) A defendant is not entitled to rely on a risk warning if the plaintiff was required to

     engage in the recreational activity by the defendant.

(10) The fact that a risk is the subject of a risk warning does not of itself mean—

     (a) that the risk is not an obvious or inherent risk of an activity, or

     (b) that a person who gives the risk warning owes a duty of care to a person who
         engages in an activity to take precautions to avoid the risk of harm from the
         activity.

(11) This section does not limit or otherwise affect the effect of a risk warning in respect
    of a risk of an activity that is not a recreational activity.

(12) In this section—

     incapable person means a person who, because of the person’s young age or a
     physical or mental disability, lacks the capacity to understand the risk warning.

     parent of an incapable person means any person (not being an incapable person)
     having parental responsibility for the incapable person.

provisions.sourceLine: s 5O  Standard of care for professionals
provisions.oneLine: A professional can rely on competent practice widely accepted by Australian peers, unless that opinion is irrational.
provisions.plain: For a professional service, the relevant practice must have been widely accepted in Australia by peer professional opinion as competent at the time of service. It need not have been universally accepted, and more than one widely accepted view may exist. The court can reject irrational peer opinion. Warning/advice liabilities require s 5P to be checked.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: Two competent schools of professional practice coexist. The existence of a different accepted approach does not alone defeat reliance on the approach actually used. But evidence of acceptance must relate to the time of the service, and irrational opinion cannot be relied on.
conditions: A person practising a profession provides a professional service.
The manner of acting was, at that time, widely accepted in Australia by peer professional opinion as competent practice.
exceptions: Peer opinion cannot be relied upon if the court considers it irrational.
Section 5P excludes the specified warning, advice and information liabilities from this Division.
limits: Universal acceptance is unnecessary.
Differing widely accepted opinions may each be relied upon.
provisions.examUse: Identify the professional practice, timing, peer evidence and irrationality issue before concluding.
pitfalls: Do not treat any expert’s personal approval as widely accepted peer practice.
Do not use s 5O to dispose of a warning claim without s 5P.
provisions.text:
(1) A person practising a profession (a professional) does not incur a liability in
    negligence arising from the provision of a professional service if it is established that
    the professional acted in a manner that (at the time the service was provided) was
    widely accepted in Australia by peer professional opinion as competent professional
    practice.

(2) However, peer professional opinion cannot be relied on for the purposes of this
    section if the court considers that the opinion is irrational.

(3) The fact that there are differing peer professional opinions widely accepted in
    Australia concerning a matter does not prevent any one or more (or all) of those
    opinions being relied on for the purposes of this section.

(4) Peer professional opinion does not have to be universally accepted to be considered
    widely accepted.

provisions.sourceLine: s 5P  Division does not apply to duty to warn of risk
provisions.oneLine: The peer-practice Division does not govern specified professional risk warnings, advice or information.
provisions.plain: Division 6 does not apply to liability connected with giving or failing to give a warning, advice or information about the risk of a person’s death or injury associated with a professional service. This keeps the warning question outside the peer-practice protection of s 5O. It does not itself establish breach or causation.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A patient challenges the lack of information about a surgical risk rather than the surgeon’s operative technique. Separate the two allegations: the warning claim is governed by its applicable warning principles, not simply by peer approval of the technique.
conditions: Liability is connected with giving or failing to give a warning, advice or other information.
The information concerns a risk of death or injury associated with provision of a professional service.
limits: It excludes the Division’s operation for the specified liability; it does not create automatic liability.
provisions.examUse: Use to separate professional performance and professional warning issues.
pitfalls: Do not treat peer acceptance as a complete answer to a failure-to-warn allegation.
provisions.text:
This Division does not apply to liability arising in connection with the giving of (or the
failure to give) a warning, advice or other information in respect of the risk of death of or
injury to a person associated with the provision by a professional of a professional service.

provisions.sourceLine: s 5Q  Liability based on non-delegable duty
provisions.oneLine: An existing non-delegable duty is measured as if liability were vicarious for the delegate’s negligence.
provisions.plain: Where a person breaches a non-delegable duty to ensure reasonable care in entrusted work, the extent of their tort liability is determined as if they were vicariously liable for the person performing that work. The section expressly applies to tort actions beyond negligence despite s 5A. It does not identify every relationship in which a non-delegable duty exists.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A school entrusts a task to another person. First establish whether the school owed the relevant non-delegable duty. If it did, analyse the delegate’s negligence and the statutory extent of the school’s liability; do not assume delegation itself discharged the duty.
conditions: A non-delegable duty to ensure reasonable care is established.
Work or a task was delegated or otherwise entrusted by the defendant.
Liability concerns negligence in connection with performance of that work or task.
limits: Applies to an action in tort whether or not it is an action in negligence.
Does not itself create a non-delegable-duty category.
provisions.examUse: After establishing the duty category, explain the statutory basis for measuring liability.
pitfalls: Do not call s 5Q a universal rule making principals liable for every independent contractor.
provisions.text:
(1) The extent of liability in tort of a person (the defendant) for breach of a non-
    delegable duty to ensure that reasonable care is taken by a person in the carrying out
    of any work or task delegated or otherwise entrusted to the person by the defendant
    is to be determined as if the liability were the vicarious liability of the defendant for
    the negligence of the person in connection with the performance of the work or task.

(2) This section applies to an action in tort whether or not it is an action in negligence,
    despite anything to the contrary in section 5A.

provisions.sourceLine: s 5R  Standard of contributory negligence
provisions.oneLine: Assess the claimant’s self-protection with negligence principles and the reasonable person in their position.
provisions.plain: Contributory negligence asks whether the injured person failed to take precautions against the risk of their own harm. Apply the negligence principles, judged against a reasonable person in the claimant’s position, using what they knew or ought to have known at the time. This is a separate inquiry from the defendant’s breach.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: An injured passenger did not use an available seatbelt. Identify what a reasonable passenger in that position would have done about the risk and what was known then; only after establishing contributory negligence consider the appropriate reduction.
conditions: A failure by the claimant to take precautions against the risk of their harm.
The reasonable-person standard in that claimant’s position.
Knowledge assessed at the relevant time.
limits: The amount of reduction is a further question, not specified by s 5R alone.
provisions.examUse: Analyse the claimant’s conduct separately, then address causation and apportionment.
pitfalls: Do not automatically find contributory negligence merely because the claimant was injured.
Do not select a percentage before explaining the conduct and its contribution.
provisions.text:
(1) The principles that are applicable in determining whether a person has been negligent
    also apply in determining whether the person who suffered harm has been

     contributorily negligent in failing to take precautions against the risk of that harm.

(2) For that purpose—

     (a) the standard of care required of the person who suffered harm is that of a
         reasonable person in the position of that person, and

     (b) the matter is to be determined on the basis of what that person knew or ought to
         have known at the time.

provisions.sourceLine: s 5S  Contributory negligence can defeat claim
provisions.oneLine: Contributory negligence can reduce damages by 100% if that is just and equitable.
provisions.plain: The court has power to make a complete reduction for contributory negligence. It must consider a 100% reduction just and equitable; the section does not require complete defeat whenever the claimant was careless. It modifies the assumption that contributory negligence can only produce a partial reduction.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A claimant’s own conduct is found overwhelmingly responsible. A complete reduction is legally available, but the answer still has to justify why 100%, rather than a smaller reduction, is just and equitable on these facts.
conditions: A reduction by reason of contributory negligence is being determined.
The court considers a 100% reduction just and equitable.
limits: The power is discretionary, not an automatic outcome.
provisions.examUse: Mention when discussing the outer limit of contributory-negligence apportionment.
pitfalls: Do not state that contributory negligence can never defeat a NSW claim.
provisions.text:
In determining the extent of a reduction in damages by reason of contributory negligence,
a court may determine a reduction of 100% if the court thinks it just and equitable to do
so, with the result that the claim for damages is defeated.

provisions.sourceLine: s 6G  Employees include persons exercising functions akin to employees
provisions.oneLine: For organisational child-abuse liability, employee includes an integral, beneficial worker akin to an employee.
provisions.plain: In this Division, an individual can count as an employee without a conventional employment contract if their activities are integral to, and benefit, the organisation. The statute excludes recognisably independent businesses and specified authorised carers, subject to regulations. This is a Division-specific expansion, not a replacement definition for all employment law.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A volunteer performs an integral role for an organisation’s benefit. That relationship can meet the akin-to-employee test even without wages. A genuinely independent business or an authorised carer acting in that capacity needs the express exclusions checked.
conditions: The individual’s activities are integral to the organisation’s activities.
Those activities benefit the organisation.
The expanded definition operates in Division 3 of Part 1B.
exceptions: Activities of a recognisably independent business are excluded.
Activities in the capacity of an authorised carer are excluded, subject to the statutory definition.
Regulations may prescribe inclusion or exclusion despite subsections (2) and (3).
limits: An authorised carer has the Care and Protection Act meaning, except a person authorised only because they are principal officer of a designated agency.
The s 6H connection with abuse must still be established.
provisions.examUse: Use for the relationship limb of Part 1B vicarious liability, keeping common-law employment analysis distinct.
pitfalls: Do not assume every volunteer or contractor is included.
Do not export this expanded definition to every vicarious-liability question.
provisions.text:
(1) In this Division—

     employee of an organisation includes an individual who is akin to an employee of the
     organisation.

(2) An individual is akin to an employee of an organisation if the individual carries out
    activities as an integral part of the activities carried on by the organisation and does
    so for the benefit of the organisation.

(3) However, an individual is not akin to an employee if—

     (a) the activities are carried out for a recognisably independent business of the
         individual or of another person or organisation, or

     (b) the activities carried on by the individual are the activities of an authorised carer
         carried on in the individual’s capacity as an authorised carer.

(4) The regulations may, despite subsections (2) and (3), prescribe circumstances in
    which an individual will be akin to an employee or not akin to an employee.

(5) In this section—

     authorised carer means a person who is an authorised carer within the meaning of
     the Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998 other than a person
     who is an authorised carer only because the person is the principal officer of a
     designated agency.

provisions.sourceLine: s 6H  Organisations vicariously liable for child abuse perpetrated by employees
provisions.oneLine: Organisational liability requires an employee’s entrusted role to supply the occasion for child abuse which the employee exploits.
provisions.plain: The organisation is vicariously liable when the apparent performance of the role in which it placed the employee supplied the occasion for the abuse, and the employee took advantage of that occasion. Consider authority, power or control, the child’s trust, and the ability to achieve intimacy. This statutory route exists in addition to the common law.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A person is placed in a trusted supervisory role over children and uses the access and authority of that role to abuse a child. Examine how the role supplied the occasion and how it was exploited; employment and opportunity in an abstract sense are not the whole analysis.
conditions: An employee, including the s 6G category.
Apparent performance of the organisationally assigned role supplies the occasion for child abuse.
The employee takes advantage of that occasion.
Consider authority/power/control, the child’s trust and ability to achieve intimacy.
limits: Child abuse means sexual or physical abuse against a child, excluding an act lawful when done.
The provision supplements rather than displaces the common law.
Commencement and temporal application must be checked where historic abuse is in issue; do not assume retrospectivity.
provisions.examUse: Structure the answer as relationship, role/occasion, exploitation, and any temporal issue.
pitfalls: Do not treat all misconduct by an employee as satisfying the role connection.
provisions.text:
(1) An organisation is vicariously liable for child abuse perpetrated against a child by an
    employee of the organisation if—

     (a) the apparent performance by the employee of a role in which the organisation
         placed the employee supplies the occasion for the perpetration of the child abuse
         by the employee, and

     (b) the employee takes advantage of that occasion to perpetrate the child abuse on
         the child.

(2) In determining if the apparent performance by the employee of a role in which the
    organisation placed the employee supplied the occasion for the perpetration of child
    abuse on a child, a court is to take into account whether the organisation placed the
    employee in a position in which the employee has one or more of the following—

     (a) authority, power or control over the child,

     (b) the trust of the child,

     (c) the ability to achieve intimacy with the child.

(3) This section does not affect, and is in addition to, the common law as it applies with
    respect to vicarious liability.

(4) In this section—

     child abuse means sexual abuse or physical abuse perpetrated against a child but
     does not include any act that is lawful at the time that it takes place.

provisions.sourceLine: s 27  Definitions
provisions.oneLine: Part 3 distinguishes standalone mental harm from mental harm consequent on another personal injury.
provisions.plain: Mental harm means impairment of mental condition. Consequential mental harm follows another kind of personal injury; pure mental harm is mental harm other than consequential mental harm. Part 3 also defines negligence and personal injury. Classifying the harm determines which later statutory restrictions need analysis.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A person develops psychiatric illness after witnessing another person’s accident but suffers no separate bodily injury: consider pure mental harm. Psychiatric consequences of that person’s own fractured leg raise consequential mental harm instead.
conditions: Mental harm: impairment of mental condition.
Consequential mental harm: consequence of another kind of personal injury.
Pure mental harm: mental harm other than consequential mental harm.
Personal injury includes prenatal injury, physical/mental impairment and disease; negligence is failure of reasonable care and skill.
limits: Definitions do not themselves prove a recognised psychiatric illness, duty or causation.
provisions.examUse: Classify the mental-harm claim before applying ss 30, 31 and 32.
pitfalls: Do not confuse the victim’s physical injury with a physical injury suffered by the claimant.
provisions.text:
In this Part—

consequential mental harm means mental harm that is a consequence of a personal
injury of any other kind.

mental harm means impairment of a person’s mental condition.

negligence means failure to exercise reasonable care and skill.

personal injury includes—

(a) pre-natal injury, and

(b) impairment of a person’s physical or mental condition, and

(c) disease.

pure mental harm means mental harm other than consequential mental harm.

provisions.sourceLine: s 29  Personal injury arising from mental or nervous shock
provisions.oneLine: Personal injury is not unrecoverable merely because it arose from mental or nervous shock.
provisions.plain: A claimant is not barred from personal-injury damages just because mental or nervous shock caused some or all of the injury. This removes a particular objection; the relevant cause of action and other applicable statutory requirements remain necessary.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A claimant’s personal injury followed shock rather than a direct physical impact. That feature alone does not prevent recovery. You still apply the applicable duty, illness, causation and other statutory requirements.
conditions: An action for personal injury.
The injury arose wholly or partly from mental or nervous shock.
limits: This is not automatic recovery for distress.
The section does not remove the other restrictions relevant to the claim.
provisions.examUse: Use when the mechanism of personal injury is mental or nervous shock.
pitfalls: Do not mistake removal of one bar for proof of every negligence element.
provisions.text:
In any action for personal injury, the plaintiff is not prevented from recovering damages
merely because the personal injury arose wholly or in part from mental or nervous shock.

provisions.sourceLine: s 30  Limitation on recovery for pure mental harm arising from shock
provisions.oneLine: Shock-connected pure mental harm requires scene witnessing or close family, with linked reductions and bars.
provisions.plain: For pure mental harm arising wholly or partly from shock connected with another person being killed, injured or put in peril by the defendant’s act or omission, the claimant must have witnessed it at the scene or be a close family member. The victim’s contributory-negligence reduction also reduces this claimant’s damages proportionately; a legal bar preventing recovery by or through the victim also prevents recovery here. The family and partner definitions must be checked precisely.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A sibling who did not witness the accident may satisfy the family route. An unrelated person must consider the scene-witness route. If the victim’s damages would be reduced for contributory negligence, subsection (3) affects the psychiatric-harm damages too.
conditions: Pure mental harm arising wholly or partly from shock in connection with another victim’s death, injury or peril caused by the defendant.
Either scene witnessing or close-family membership.

Close family includes a parent or person with parental responsibility; spouse/partner; child, stepchild or anyone for whom the victim has parental responsibility; brother, sister, half-brother, half-sister, stepbrother or stepsister.
exceptions: A bar to recovery by or through the victim under written or unwritten law also bars these damages.
limits: Reduce damages in the same proportion as the victim’s contributory-negligence reduction.
Spouse/partner includes legal spouse or de facto partner, with only the last person qualifying where more than one otherwise qualifies.
Do not treat the section as applying to every mental-harm claim irrespective of its opening conditions.
provisions.examUse: Check scope, gateway, definitions, linked reduction and linked bar in that order.
pitfalls: Do not stop at subsection (2).
Do not substitute friend, cousin or any relative for the statutory close-family definition.
provisions.text:
(1) This section applies to the liability of a person (the defendant) for pure mental harm
    to a person (the plaintiff) arising wholly or partly from mental or nervous shock in
    connection with another person (the victim) being killed, injured or put in peril by the
    act or omission of the defendant.

(2) The plaintiff is not entitled to recover damages for pure mental harm unless—

     (a) the plaintiff witnessed, at the scene, the victim being killed, injured or put in peril,
         or

     (b) the plaintiff is a close member of the family of the victim.

(3) Any damages to be awarded to the plaintiff for pure mental harm are to be reduced in
    the same proportion as any reduction in the damages that may be recovered from the
    defendant by or through the victim on the basis of the contributory negligence of the
    victim.

(4) No damages are to be awarded to the plaintiff for pure mental harm if the recovery of
    damages from the defendant by or through the victim in respect of the act or omission
    would be prevented by any provision of this Act or any other written or unwritten law.

(5) In this section—

     close member of the family of a victim means—

     (a) a parent of the victim or other person with parental responsibility for the victim, or

     (b) the spouse or partner of the victim, or

     (c) a child or stepchild of the victim or any other person for whom the victim has
         parental responsibility, or

     (d) a brother, sister, half-brother or half-sister, or stepbrother or stepsister of the
         victim.

     spouse or partner means—

     (a) the person to whom the victim is legally married (including the husband or wife of
         the victim), or

     (b) a de facto partner,

     but where more than one person would so qualify as a spouse or partner, means only
     the last person to so qualify.

provisions.sourceLine: s 31  Pure mental harm—liability only for recognised psychiatric illness
provisions.oneLine: Pure mental harm from negligence must be a recognised psychiatric illness.
provisions.plain: Grief, fear and distress alone do not satisfy this damages threshold for pure mental harm resulting from negligence. The harm must consist of a recognised psychiatric illness. Establishing that illness still leaves duty, causation and the other applicable requirements to prove.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A witness is deeply upset after an accident. That alone does not establish s 31. Evidence that the witness has a recognised psychiatric illness is needed before this statutory damages threshold is satisfied.
conditions: Pure mental harm resulting from negligence.
The harm consists of a recognised psychiatric illness.
limits: A diagnostic threshold is not proof of a duty or factual causation.
provisions.examUse: Address early so ordinary distress is not analysed as an established psychiatric-injury claim.
pitfalls: Do not equate severe emotions with a legally recognised psychiatric illness.
provisions.text:
There is no liability to pay damages for pure mental harm resulting from negligence
unless the harm consists of a recognised psychiatric illness.

provisions.sourceLine: s 32  Mental harm—duty of care
provisions.oneLine: Mental-harm duty depends on foreseeable recognised psychiatric illness, considering the claimant’s circumstances and known fortitude.
provisions.plain: The defendant must have been able to foresee that a person of normal fortitude might suffer recognised psychiatric illness if reasonable care were not taken. For pure harm, the statute identifies shock, scene witnessing and relevant relationships as circumstances, rather than compulsory standalone elements. For consequential harm, consider the personal injury. Known vulnerability is not to be ignored.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: An employer knows a worker is particularly vulnerable and sends them into a traumatic situation. The normal-fortitude formulation does not require the court to disregard that knowledge. Analyse the actual circumstances and any relevant relationship.
conditions: Foreseeability of recognised psychiatric illness to a person of normal fortitude in the circumstances if care were not taken.
For pure mental harm, consider sudden shock, scene witnessing, claimant–victim relationship and any pre-existing claimant–defendant relationship.
For consequential mental harm, consider the claimant’s personal injury.
limits: Subsection (4) preserves what the defendant knew or ought to have known about the claimant’s fortitude.
The listed circumstances are not a rigid four-element checklist.
provisions.examUse: Explain the foreseeable psychiatric consequence and weigh the relevant statutory circumstances.
pitfalls: Do not demand sudden shock or direct perception in every s 32 claim.
Do not ignore known susceptibility.
provisions.text:
(1) A person (the defendant) does not owe a duty of care to another person (the
    plaintiff) to take care not to cause the plaintiff mental harm unless the defendant
    ought to have foreseen that a person of normal fortitude might, in the circumstances
    of the case, suffer a recognised psychiatric illness if reasonable care were not taken.

(2) For the purposes of the application of this section in respect of pure mental harm, the
    circumstances of the case include the following—

     (a) whether or not the mental harm was suffered as the result of a sudden shock,

     (b) whether the plaintiff witnessed, at the scene, a person being killed, injured or put
         in peril,

     (c) the nature of the relationship between the plaintiff and any person killed, injured
         or put in peril,

     (d) whether or not there was a pre-existing relationship between the plaintiff and the
         defendant.

(3) For the purposes of the application of this section in respect of consequential mental
    harm, the circumstances of the case include the personal injury suffered by the
    plaintiff.

(4) This section does not require the court to disregard what the defendant knew or ought
    to have known about the fortitude of the plaintiff.

provisions.sourceLine: s 34  Application of Part
provisions.oneLine: Part 4 is limited to defined economic/property claims and concurrent wrongdoers, excluding personal-injury claims.
provisions.plain: Proportionate liability applies to the specified economic-loss or property-damage claims arising from a failure to take reasonable care, and to the specified misleading-conduct claims. Subsection (1)(a) excludes any claim arising out of personal injury. Multiple causes of action for the same loss form a single apportionable claim. Insolvency, winding-up, cessation of existence or death of a concurrent wrongdoer does not prevent the Part operating. The specified Home Building Act statutory-warranty claims are excluded.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: Two advisers independently contribute to the same investment loss. First test whether the claim is apportionable under s 34. A separate bodily-injury claim cannot simply be placed in the same scheme, and a Home Building Act statutory-warranty claim needs its express exclusion checked.
conditions: A claim within subsection (1): specified careless economic/property loss, or the listed Fair Trading/ACL misleading-conduct category.
Concurrent wrongdoers are two or more persons whose acts or omissions caused the same loss, independently or jointly.
The same loss forms one apportionable claim despite multiple causes of action.
exceptions: Personal-injury claims are excluded from subsection (1)(a).
Specified Part 2C Home Building Act 1989 statutory-warranty claims brought by a beneficiary are excluded by subsection (3A).
limits: Only subsection (1) claims are apportionable.
Insolvency, winding-up, cessation of existence or death of a wrongdoer does not prevent operation.
The full text preserves the historical Fair Trading Act reference alongside ACL (NSW) s 18.
provisions.examUse: Determine the scope of Part 4 before apportioning liability under s 35.
pitfalls: Do not apply proportionate liability to all multiple-defendant negligence claims.
Do not confuse contribution between tortfeasors with liability limited at the claimant-facing stage.
provisions.text:
(1) This Part applies to the following claims (apportionable claims)—

      (a) a claim for economic loss or damage to property in an action for damages
          (whether in contract, tort or otherwise) arising from a failure to take reasonable
          care, but not including any claim arising out of personal injury,

      (b) a claim for economic loss or damage to property in an action for damages under
          the Fair Trading Act 1987 for a contravention of section 42 of that Act (as in force
          before its repeal by the Fair Trading Amendment (Australian Consumer Law) Act
          2010) or under the Australian Consumer Law (NSW) for a contravention of section
          18 of that Law.

(1A) For the purposes of this Part, there is a single apportionable claim in proceedings in
    respect of the same loss or damage even if the claim for the loss or damage is based
    on more than one cause of action (whether or not of the same or a different kind).

(2) In this Part, a concurrent wrongdoer, in relation to a claim, is a person who is one
    of two or more persons whose acts or omissions (or act or omission) caused,
    independently of each other or jointly, the damage or loss that is the subject of the
    claim.

(3) For the purposes of this Part, apportionable claims are limited to those claims
    specified in subsection (1).

(3A) This Part does not apply to a claim in an action for damages arising from a breach of
    statutory warranty under Part 2C of the Home Building Act 1989 and brought by a
    person having the benefit of the statutory warranty.

(4) For the purposes of this Part it does not matter that a concurrent wrongdoer is
    insolvent, is being wound up or has ceased to exist or died.

(5)    (Repealed)

provisions.sourceLine: s 35  Proportionate liability for apportionable claims
provisions.oneLine: For an apportionable claim, each concurrent wrongdoer’s liability is capped at the responsibility share the court finds just.
provisions.plain: Once Part 4 applies, the defendant’s liability is limited to a just share reflecting their responsibility. Separate apportionable from non-apportionable claims, remove the claimant’s contributory-negligence proportion before apportioning among defendants, and consider other concurrent wrongdoers even if they are not parties. The statute does not prescribe an automatic numerical formula.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: After excluding the claimant’s own share, the court evaluates each adviser’s responsibility for the remaining economic loss. An absent or insolvent concurrent wrongdoer does not automatically cause the sued adviser to pay that missing share under this Part.
conditions: An apportionable claim under s 34.
The defendant is a concurrent wrongdoer.
Judgment does not exceed the amount reflecting the just responsibility proportion.
Exclude the claimant’s contributory-negligence proportion in apportioning between defendants.
limits: Mixed proceedings require different treatment of non-apportionable claims.
The court may consider a concurrent wrongdoer who is not a party; not all need be joined.
Defendant includes a joined defendant or other party except a plaintiff.
provisions.examUse: Explain the order of reductions and why the selected shares reflect responsibility.
pitfalls: Do not make up percentages without factual reasoning.
Do not treat the example calculation as a judicial outcome prediction.
provisions.text:
(1) In any proceedings involving an apportionable claim—

     (a) the liability of a defendant who is a concurrent wrongdoer in relation to that claim
         is limited to an amount reflecting that proportion of the damage or loss claimed
         that the court considers just having regard to the extent of the defendant’s
         responsibility for the damage or loss, and

     (b) the court may give judgment against the defendant for not more than that
         amount.

(2) If the proceedings involve both an apportionable claim and a claim that is not an
    apportionable claim—

     (a) liability for the apportionable claim is to be determined in accordance with the
         provisions of this Part, and

     (b) liability for the other claim is to be determined in accordance with the legal rules,
         if any, that (apart from this Part) are relevant.

(3) In apportioning responsibility between defendants in the proceedings—

     (a) the court is to exclude that proportion of the damage or loss in relation to which
         the plaintiff is contributorily negligent under any relevant law, and

     (b) the court may have regard to the comparative responsibility of any concurrent
         wrongdoer who is not a party to the proceedings.

(4) This section applies in proceedings involving an apportionable claim whether or not all
    concurrent wrongdoers are parties to the proceedings.

(5) A reference in this Part to a defendant in proceedings includes any person joined as a
    defendant or other party in the proceedings (except as a plaintiff) whether joined
    under this Part, under rules of court or otherwise.

provisions.sourceLine: s 41  Definitions
provisions.oneLine: Part 5 defines public authorities and functions broadly, including specified public-official roles.
provisions.plain: Public or other authority includes the Crown, government departments, public health organisations, local councils, statutory public/local authorities, and the specified regulatory categories. A person with public-official functions can qualify in relation to those functions even without public employment. Function includes powers, authorities and duties; exercising a function includes performing a duty.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A private individual exercises a statutory public-official function. Ask whether the claim concerns that function before deciding whether the person falls within Part 5; their private activities are not automatically covered.
conditions: Identify a category in the statutory definition.
For the public-official-function category, connect the relevant conduct to that function.
Check any applicable prescribed persons, bodies, functions or classes.
limits: Status as a covered authority does not automatically establish every Part 5 protection.
The definitions of function and exercise extend to duties.
provisions.examUse: Identify the defendant and relevant function before applying ss 42–46.
pitfalls: Do not restrict Part 5 only to conventional government employees.
Do not assume all acts by an official are covered.
provisions.text:
In this Part—

exercise a function includes perform a duty.

function includes a power, authority or duty.

public or other authority means—

(a) the Crown (within the meaning of the Crown Proceedings Act 1988), or

(b) a Government department, or

(c) a public health organisation within the meaning of the Health Services Act 1997, or

(d) a local council, or

(e) any public or local authority constituted by or under an Act, or

(e1) any person having public official functions or acting in a public official capacity
    (whether or not employed as a public official), but only in relation to the exercise of
    the person’s public official functions, or

(f) a person or body prescribed (or of a class prescribed) by the regulations as an
    authority to which this Part applies (in respect of all or specified functions), or

(g) any person or body in respect of the exercise of public or other functions of a class
    prescribed by the regulations for the purposes of this Part.

provisions.sourceLine: s 42  Principles concerning resources, responsibilities etc of public or other authorities
provisions.oneLine: Duty and breach for authorities account for available resources, general allocation, whole responsibilities and compliance evidence.
provisions.plain: What an authority must do is limited by reasonably available financial and other resources. The general allocation of those resources is not open to challenge. Assess its functions against its broad range of activities rather than this problem alone. Evidence of compliance with general procedures and applicable standards can support proper performance, but is evidence rather than an automatic conclusion.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A council has many facilities requiring inspection. Assess the proposed inspection burden against its available resources and broad responsibilities, rather than assuming all resources should have been concentrated on the place where this accident occurred.
conditions: The principles operate when determining duty or breach in relevant Part 5 proceedings.
Consider reasonably available financial and other resources.
Do not challenge general resource allocation.
Consider the broad range of the authority’s activities.
The authority may rely on compliance evidence.
limits: The section does not itself mean an authority can never be negligent.
Compliance evidence is not expressed as conclusive proof.
provisions.examUse: Apply to both duty and breach where relevant, tying each resource claim to the evidence.
pitfalls: Do not turn limited resources into an unexplained blanket immunity.
provisions.text:
The following principles apply in determining whether a public or other authority has a
duty of care or has breached a duty of care in proceedings for civil liability to which this
Part applies—

(a) the functions required to be exercised by the authority are limited by the financial and
    other resources that are reasonably available to the authority for the purpose of
    exercising those functions,

(b) the general allocation of those resources by the authority is not open to challenge,

(c) the functions required to be exercised by the authority are to be determined by
    reference to the broad range of its activities (and not merely by reference to the
    matter to which the proceedings relate),

(d) the authority may rely on evidence of its compliance with the general procedures and
    applicable standards for the exercise of its functions as evidence of the proper
    exercise of its functions in the matter to which the proceedings relate.

provisions.sourceLine: s 43  Proceedings against public or other authorities based on breach of statutory duty
provisions.oneLine: Breach-of-statutory-duty proceedings against an authority require the specified very unreasonable conduct threshold.
provisions.plain: Where the liability is based on breach of an authority’s statutory duty, an act or omission does not breach that duty unless it was so unreasonable that no authority with those functions could properly view it as a reasonable exercise. This is more demanding than simply finding a better available course. Regulatory functions also require s 44.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A claimant argues that a council breached a statutory duty to act. It is not enough to say the claimant would have preferred more action: explain why no authority with those functions could properly consider this response reasonable.
conditions: Relevant civil liability is based on breach of statutory duty.
The conduct is connected with exercise or failure to exercise an authority function.
Apply the statutory so-unreasonable threshold.
limits: The cause of action and statutory duty must first be identified.
For prohibition/regulation functions, s 44 applies in addition.
provisions.examUse: Use for statutory-duty liability; distinguish it from ordinary negligence and the special-power question.
pitfalls: Do not cite s 43 as if every negligence claim against an authority were necessarily a breach-of-statutory-duty action.
provisions.text:
(1) This section applies to proceedings for civil liability to which this Part applies to the
    extent that the liability is based on a breach of a statutory duty by a public or other
    authority in connection with the exercise of or a failure to exercise a function of the
    authority.

(2) For the purposes of any such proceedings, an act or omission of the authority does
    not constitute a breach of statutory duty unless the act or omission was in the
    circumstances so unreasonable that no authority having the functions of the authority
    in question could properly consider the act or omission to be a reasonable exercise of
    its functions.

(3) In the case of a function of a public or other authority to prohibit or regulate an
    activity, this section applies in addition to section 44.

provisions.sourceLine: s 43A  Proceedings against public or other authorities for the exercise of special statutory powers
provisions.oneLine: Special statutory powers attract a stringent unreasonableness threshold for relevant civil liability.
provisions.plain: A special statutory power is conferred by statute and is of a kind ordinary people cannot exercise without specific statutory authority. Liability based on exercising or failing to exercise such a power requires conduct so unreasonable that no authority with that power could properly consider it reasonable. The statute covers both action and inaction.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: Issuing a statutory licence can involve a special power. Putting up an ordinary barrier may be something anyone can do. Identify the actual power before applying the stringent threshold; do not rely solely on the defendant being a council.
conditions: A power conferred by or under statute.
A kind of power people generally cannot exercise without specific statutory authority.
Liability is based on its exercise or non-exercise.
The act/omission satisfies the statutory so-unreasonable threshold.
limits: For prohibition/regulation powers, s 44 operates in addition.
A statutory source alone does not satisfy the second limb of special statutory power.
provisions.examUse: Identify the source and character of the precise power before applying subsection (3).
pitfalls: Do not call every activity of a statutory authority a special statutory power.
provisions.text:
(1) This section applies to proceedings for civil liability to which this Part applies to the
    extent that the liability is based on a public or other authority’s exercise of, or failure
    to exercise, a special statutory power conferred on the authority.

(2) A special statutory power is a power—

     (a) that is conferred by or under a statute, and

     (b) that is of a kind that persons generally are not authorised to exercise without
         specific statutory authority.

(3) For the purposes of any such proceedings, any act or omission involving an exercise
    of, or failure to exercise, a special statutory power does not give rise to civil liability
    unless the act or omission was in the circumstances so unreasonable that no authority
    having the special statutory power in question could properly consider the act or
    omission to be a reasonable exercise of, or failure to exercise, its power.

(4) In the case of a special statutory power of a public or other authority to prohibit or
    regulate an activity, this section applies in addition to section 44.
