provisions.sourceLine: s 44  When public or other authority not liable for failure to exercise regulatory functions
provisions.oneLine: An authority is protected for relevant regulatory inaction if this claimant could not have compelled it to act.
provisions.plain: For a claim based on failure to prohibit or regulate an activity, the authority is not liable if proceedings by the claimant could not have required exercise of the function. Regulatory functions expressly include licensing, permits, registration and other authorisation. This is a particular protection for failure to act, not a general rule about every negligent positive act.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A claimant says the authority should have revoked another person’s licence. Ask whether that claimant could have required the authority to exercise the function in proceedings; do not assume the existence of a power created an enforceable obligation.
conditions: Liability is based on failure to exercise or consider exercising a prohibition/regulation function.
The authority could not have been required to exercise it in proceedings instituted by this claimant.
limits: Licensing, permits, registration and authorisation fall within regulation.
Sections 43 and 43A can operate alongside this protection.
provisions.examUse: Analyse the claimant’s ability to compel action and the nature of the regulatory failure.
pitfalls: Do not equate discretion to regulate with a privately enforceable duty to do so.
provisions.text:
(1) A public or other authority is not liable in proceedings for civil liability to which this
    Part applies to the extent that the liability is based on the failure of the authority to
    exercise or to consider exercising any function of the authority to prohibit or regulate
    an activity if the authority could not have been required to exercise the function in
    proceedings instituted by the plaintiff.

(2) Without limiting what constitutes a function to regulate an activity for the purposes of
    this section, a function to issue a licence, permit or other authority in respect of an
    activity, or to register or otherwise authorise a person in connection with an activity,
    constitutes a function to regulate the activity.

provisions.sourceLine: s 45  Special non-feasance protection for roads authorities
provisions.oneLine: Roads-authority non-feasance protection requires actual knowledge of the particular risk before the statutory bar can be displaced.
provisions.plain: A roads authority is protected for failure to carry out or consider road work unless it actually knew, at the relevant time, of the particular risk that materialised. Merely showing what it ought to have known is insufficient for this exception. Actual knowledge does not itself create a duty or change the otherwise applicable standard of care.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A pothole causes injury. Distinguish a failure to inspect or repair from negligent positive work, and identify evidence that the relevant authority actually knew of this particular risk before the failure. General awareness that roads deteriorate is not the stated test.
conditions: A roads authority as defined by the Roads Act 1993.
Harm from failure to carry out or consider road work.
Exception requires actual knowledge, at that time, of the particular risk that materialised.
limits: Actual knowledge neither creates a duty by itself nor changes the applicable standard.

Carry out road work includes any activity connected with construction, erection, installation, maintenance, inspection, repair, removal or replacement of a road work within the Roads Act 1993 meaning.
provisions.examUse: Separate non-feasance, actual knowledge, duty and breach; use the supplied case treatment for whose knowledge counts.
pitfalls: Do not replace actual knowledge with ought to have known.
Do not treat knowledge as automatic liability.
provisions.text:
(1) A roads authority is not liable in proceedings for civil liability to which this Part applies

     for harm arising from a failure of the authority to carry out road work, or to consider
     carrying out road work, unless at the time of the alleged failure the authority had
     actual knowledge of the particular risk the materialisation of which resulted in the
     harm.

(2) This section does not operate—

     (a) to create a duty of care in respect of a risk merely because a roads authority has
         actual knowledge of the risk, or

     (b) to affect any standard of care that would otherwise be applicable in respect of a
         risk.

(3) In this section—

     carry out road work means carry out any activity in connection with the
     construction, erection, installation, maintenance, inspection, repair, removal or
     replacement of a road work within the meaning of the Roads Act 1993.

     roads authority has the same meaning as in the Roads Act 1993.

provisions.sourceLine: s 46  Exercise of function or decision to exercise does not create duty
provisions.oneLine: Exercising or deciding to exercise a function does not itself establish a duty about exercising it.
provisions.plain: An authority’s choice to act, or its prior exercise of a power, does not alone show that it had a duty to exercise the function in those circumstances or in a particular way. Other facts and legal principles may still establish a duty or breach; this section simply prevents the choice itself doing all the work.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A council once inspected a site. That fact alone does not establish a duty to inspect on every later occasion. Look for the relationship, statutory framework and other relevant features instead.
conditions: Proceedings to which Part 5 applies.
Reliance on exercise or a decision to exercise a function as indicating a duty.
limits: The words of itself preserve a wider contextual duty analysis.
provisions.examUse: Use when the argument relies on the authority having acted or chosen to act before.
pitfalls: Do not infer a complete immunity from a provision that rejects only one automatic inference.
provisions.text:
In proceedings to which this Part applies, the fact that a public or other authority exercises
or decides to exercise a function does not of itself indicate that the authority is under a
duty to exercise the function or that the function should be exercised in particular
circumstances or in a particular way.

provisions.sourceLine: s 50  No recovery where person intoxicated
provisions.oneLine: Impairing intoxication can bar recovery or trigger at least a 25% reduction, subject to the statutory qualifications.
provisions.plain: The relevant intoxicated person is the person whose death, injury or damage is the subject of the proceedings, which may differ from the person bringing the claim. If intoxication impaired that person’s capacity for reasonable care and skill at the causative act or omission, damages are barred unless the court is satisfied that the death, injury or property damage—or some other injury or property damage—was likely even without intoxication. If that hurdle is passed, contributory negligence is presumed unless the court is satisfied that intoxication contributed in no way. Where the presumption applies, the reduction is at least 25%. The section does not apply if the court is satisfied that intoxication was not self-induced.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: An intoxicated pedestrian proves an unavoidable collision was likely even if sober. Recovery is not automatically intact: determine whether intoxication contributed in any way and whether the statutory presumption and minimum reduction apply.
conditions: At the time of the causative act or omission, the person whose death, injury or damage is in issue was intoxicated to the extent that capacity for reasonable care and skill was impaired.
To recover, establish the statutory likely-even-if-sober counterfactual.
If recovery survives, test the contributory-negligence presumption.
exceptions: The presumption can be displaced if intoxication did not contribute in any way.
The section does not apply where the court is satisfied intoxication was not self-induced.
limits: The minimum 25% reduction operates when the presumption applies, not in every case involving alcohol.
The precise counterfactual wording includes some other injury or property damage.
provisions.examUse: Apply the bar, presumption and percentage stages in order, preserving subsection (5).
pitfalls: Do not impose a universal 25% discount merely because the claimant drank.
Do not skip the initial recovery hurdle.
provisions.text:
(1) This section applies when it is established that the person whose death, injury or
    damage is the subject of proceedings for the recovery of damages was at the time of
    the act or omission that caused the death, injury or damage intoxicated to the extent
    that the person’s capacity to exercise reasonable care and skill was impaired.

(2) A court is not to award damages in respect of liability to which this Part applies unless
    satisfied that the death, injury or damage to property (or some other injury or damage
    to property) is likely to have occurred even if the person had not been intoxicated.

(3) If the court is satisfied that the death, injury or damage to property (or some other
    injury or damage to property) is likely to have occurred even if the person had not
    been intoxicated, it is to be presumed that the person was contributorily negligent
    unless the court is satisfied that the person’s intoxication did not contribute in any
    way to the cause of the death, injury or damage.

(4) When there is a presumption of contributory negligence, the court must assess
    damages on the basis that the damages to which the person would be entitled in the
    absence of contributory negligence are to be reduced on account of contributory
    negligence by 25% or a greater percentage determined by the court to be appropriate
    in the circumstances of the case.

(5) This section does not apply in a case where the court is satisfied that the intoxication
    was not self-induced.

provisions.sourceLine: s 54  Criminals not to be awarded damages
provisions.oneLine: A materially contributing serious offence by the claimant can bar damages, except where the defendant’s causative conduct is an offence.
provisions.plain: The bar concerns conduct of the person whose death, injury or damage is the subject of the proceedings. That harm must occur at the time of or after conduct that, on the balance of probabilities, constitutes an offence punishable by at least six months’ imprisonment; the conduct must materially contribute to the harm or its risk. The bar does not apply against a defendant whose causative conduct constitutes any offence, serious or otherwise. Criminal proceedings and conviction are unnecessary, including where prosecution is not possible. The Felons (Civil Proceedings) Act 1981 remains unaffected.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A claimant is hurt during conduct punishable by six months or more. Do not stop at criminality: assess material contribution and whether the defendant’s conduct causing the injury was also an offence. The latter offence need not itself be serious.
conditions: The relevant person is the person whose death, injury or damage is the subject of the proceedings; that person’s conduct constitutes a serious offence on the balance of probabilities.
The harm occurred at the time of or following that conduct.
The conduct materially contributed to the harm or its risk.
exceptions: The section does not apply where the defendant’s causative conduct constitutes an offence, serious or otherwise.
limits: A serious offence is punishable by six months’ imprisonment or more.
The section operates whether or not a person whose conduct is alleged to be an offence has been, will be, or is capable of being proceeded against or convicted.
The Felons (Civil Proceedings) Act 1981 is unaffected.
The source note says ss 52 and 53 can still prevent or limit recovery despite the defendant’s offence; those provisions are contextual, not added to the examinable filter.
provisions.examUse: Analyse statutory seriousness, timing, material contribution and the defendant-offence exception separately.
pitfalls: Do not treat any illegality as automatically barring recovery.
Do not demand a criminal conviction.
provisions.text:
(1) A court is not to award damages in respect of liability to which this Part applies if the
    court is satisfied that—

     (a) the death of, or the injury or damage to, the person that is the subject of the
         proceedings occurred at the time of, or following, conduct of that person that, on
         the balance of probabilities, constitutes a serious offence, and

     (b) that conduct contributed materially to the death, injury or damage or to the risk of
         death, injury or damage.

(2) This section does not apply to an award of damages against a defendant if the
    conduct of the defendant that caused the death, injury or damage concerned
    constitutes an offence (whether or not a serious offence).

(3) A serious offence is an offence punishable by imprisonment for 6 months or more.

(4) This section does not affect the operation of the Felons (Civil Proceedings) Act 1981.

(5) This section operates whether or not a person whose conduct is alleged to constitute
    an offence has been, will be or is capable of being proceeded against or convicted of
    any offence concerned.

provisions.sourceLine: s 55  Application of Part
provisions.oneLine: The good-samaritan Part applies to civil liability of any kind, subject to s 3B exclusions.
provisions.plain: Part 8 is not confined by its application clause to negligence as a cause of action. However, any liability excluded from this Part by s 3B remains outside it. The application clause is only the entry point: the definition, emergency protection and exclusions in ss 56–58 still need analysis.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A claim against a volunteer is given a legal label other than negligence. Check Part 8’s broad application and s 3B before assuming that label avoids the good-samaritan provisions.
conditions: Civil liability of any kind.
No applicable s 3B exclusion from this Part.
exceptions: Liability excluded by s 3B remains excluded.
limits: This provision alone does not confer immunity.
provisions.examUse: Use before the definition and protection in ss 56–58.
pitfalls: Do not assume every volunteer is protected just because Part 8 applies.
provisions.text:
(1) This Part applies to civil liability of any kind.

(2) This Part does not apply to civil liability that is excluded from the operation of this Part

provisions.sourceLine: s 56  Who is a good samaritan
provisions.oneLine: A good samaritan helps an apparently injured or endangered person in good faith without expecting reward.
provisions.plain: The definition requires good faith, no expectation of payment or other reward, and assistance to someone apparently injured or at risk of injury. It is not confined to medically qualified people. Meeting this definition is the first step; the emergency protection and its exclusions must then be considered.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: An off-duty nurse voluntarily helps a stranger who appears injured and expects no payment. She may meet the definition. A paid on-duty response or a person acting for reward needs different analysis.
conditions: Good faith.
No expectation of payment or other reward.
Assistance to a person apparently injured or at risk of being injured.
limits: Meeting the definition does not dispense with the emergency requirement in s 57 or the exclusions in s 58.
provisions.examUse: Establish the rescuer’s status before applying the personal-liability protection.
pitfalls: Do not make professional qualifications or a pre-existing friendship prerequisites.
Do not call self-rescue assistance to another.
provisions.text:
For the purposes of this Part, a good samaritan is a person who, in good faith and
without expectation of payment or other reward, comes to the assistance of a person who
is apparently injured or at risk of being injured.

provisions.sourceLine: s 57  Protection of good samaritans
provisions.oneLine: A good samaritan receives personal civil-liability protection for emergency assistance, without removing another person’s vicarious liability.
provisions.plain: A person meeting s 56 is protected personally for acts or omissions in an emergency while helping someone apparently injured or endangered. The protection must be read with s 58. It does not affect another person’s vicarious liability for the rescuer’s acts or omissions.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A genuine unpaid rescuer makes a careless mistake while providing emergency help. Personal liability may be protected, but examine the exclusions and keep any other person’s vicarious liability separate.
conditions: A good samaritan under s 56.
An act or omission in an emergency.
Assistance to someone apparently injured or at risk.
exceptions: Section 58 removes protection in its specified circumstances.
limits: Only the rescuer’s personal liability is protected; subsection (2) preserves another person’s vicarious liability.
provisions.examUse: Apply after the definition, then test each exclusion that the facts raise.
pitfalls: Do not omit subsection (2).
Do not assume every non-emergency volunteer service falls within this section.
provisions.text:
(1) A good samaritan does not incur any personal civil liability in respect of any act or
    omission done or made by the good samaritan in an emergency when assisting a
    person who is apparently injured or at risk of being injured.

(2) This section does not affect the vicarious liability of any other person for the acts or
    omissions of the good samaritan.

provisions.sourceLine: s 58  Exclusion from protection
provisions.oneLine: Good-samaritan protection is lost for a self-created danger, specified impairing intoxication plus lack of care, or false emergency expertise.
provisions.plain: The protection does not cover a person whose intentional or negligent act or omission caused the original injury or risk. A second exclusion requires both significant impairment from voluntarily consumed alcohol/drugs and failure of reasonable care and skill. A third excludes impersonation of emergency/health/police personnel or false claims of relevant emergency skills. Voluntary medication can fall within the intoxication wording.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A helper whose intentional or negligent act caused the original injury or risk cannot rely on this protection. For a helper who voluntarily consumed medication, assess both significant impairment and failure of reasonable care and skill; drug use alone is insufficient. A person falsely claiming to be a paramedic raises the separate impersonation or false-skills exclusion.
conditions: Exclusion (1): the helper’s intentional or negligent act/omission caused the injury or risk initially assisted.
Exclusion (2): voluntary alcohol/drug consumption significantly impaired care and skill, and the helper failed to use reasonable care and skill.
Exclusion (3): the act/omission occurred while impersonating specified workers or falsely claiming relevant emergency skills/expertise.
limits: Voluntarily consumed drugs include medication for subsection (2).
Mere consumption does not satisfy both limbs of subsection (2).
Loss of statutory protection is not itself proof of all elements of a tort.
provisions.examUse: Test all factually raised exclusions without turning them into automatic tort liability.
pitfalls: Do not omit subsection (3).
Do not say any alcohol or medication automatically removes protection.
provisions.text:
(1) The protection from personal liability conferred by this Part does not apply if it is the
    good samaritan’s intentional or negligent act or omission that caused the injury or risk
    of injury in respect of which the good samaritan first comes to the assistance of the
    person.

(2) The protection from personal liability conferred by this Part in respect of an act or
    omission does not apply if—

     (a) the ability of the good samaritan to exercise reasonable care and skill was
         significantly impaired by reason of the good samaritan being under the influence
         of alcohol or a drug voluntarily consumed (whether or not it was consumed for
         medication), and

     (b) the good samaritan failed to exercise reasonable care and skill in connection with
         the act or omission.

(3) This Part does not confer protection from personal liability on a person in respect of
    any act or omission done or made while the person is impersonating a health care or
    emergency services worker or a police officer or is otherwise falsely representing that
    the person has skills or expertise in connection with the rendering of emergency
    assistance.

provisions.sourceLine: s 5  Proceedings against and contribution between joint and several tort-feasors
provisions.oneLine: Section 5 regulates successive judgments, contribution between tortfeasors and the court’s power to allocate responsibility.
provisions.plain: A judgment against one joint tortfeasor does not itself bar an action against another for the same damage. For the multiple actions specified in (1)(b), total damages cannot exceed the first judgment, and later-action costs need reasonable grounds. A liable tortfeasor may seek contribution from another who is or would have been liable for the same damage. The court allocates a just and equitable amount by responsibility, and may order no contribution or a complete indemnity. Indemnity obligations, appeal-adjusted judgments, Crown liability and the temporal rules must be checked.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A claimant obtains a judgment against one of two jointly liable companies. Section 5(1)(a) permits a further action against the other, while (1)(b) limits aggregate damages and later-action costs. If one company seeks contribution, the court assesses responsibility rather than mechanically splitting the bill. It may exempt the other company or order a complete indemnity, but cannot grant contribution against a person whom the contributor is itself obliged to indemnify. If the first judgment is reversed or varied on appeal, use the adjusted statutory meaning of the first judgment.
conditions: Damage was suffered as a result of a tort, whether or not also a crime.
Subsection (1)(a): the first judgment and later action concern the same damage, and the later defendant would, if sued, have been liable as a joint tortfeasor.

Subsection (1)(b): more than one action is brought by/on behalf of the injured person, or for the benefit of the estate, spouse, brother, sister, half-brother, half-sister, parent or child, against tortfeasors liable for the damage, jointly or otherwise.
Subsection (1)(c): the contributor and the other tortfeasor are, or the latter would if sued have been, liable for the same damage, jointly or otherwise.
Contribution is just and equitable having regard to the extent of responsibility for the damage; the court may exempt a person or order a complete indemnity.
Parent and child carry the Compensation to Relatives Act 1897 meanings. Spouse includes the de facto partner at death.
Where Crown vicarious liability arises under s 8 of the Law Reform (Vicarious Liability) Act 1983, Crown and tortfeasor are joint tortfeasors for this section.
exceptions: No contribution may be recovered from a person whom the claimant for contribution must indemnify in respect of that liability.
Later-action costs under (1)(b) require the court to consider there was reasonable ground for bringing that action.
A reversed first judgment is replaced by the first judgment not reversed; a varied judgment is read as varied.
limits: In the multiple actions within (1)(b), aggregate damages cannot exceed the damages awarded by the first judgment, read with the appeal rule in (3)(b).
The section does not apply to torts committed before commencement of Part 3.
The Crown/person joint-tortfeasor rule does not apply to the specified pre-commencement torts governed by s 8 of the Law Reform (Vicarious Liability) Act 1983.
The section leaves criminal proceedings unaffected and does not make an otherwise unenforceable indemnity agreement enforceable.
The 2002 relationships amendments do not apply where the tort occurred before their commencement.

provisions.examUse: Distinguish claimant-facing liability, contribution and indemnity.
pitfalls: Do not confuse contribution with Part 4 proportionate liability.
provisions.text:
(1) Where damage is suffered by any person as a result of a tort (whether a crime or not):

(a) judgment recovered against any tort-feasor liable in respect of that damage shall not be a bar to an action against any other person who would, if sued, have been liable as a joint tort-feasor in respect of the same damage,

(b) if more than one action is brought in respect of that damage by or on behalf of the person by whom it was suffered, or for the benefit of the estate, or of the spouse, brother, sister, half-brother, half-sister, parent or child, of that person, against tort-feasors liable in respect of the damage (whether as joint tort-feasors or otherwise) the sums recoverable under the judgments given in those actions by way of damages shall not in the aggregate exceed the amount of the damages awarded by the judgment first given; and in any of those actions, other than that in which judgment is first given, the plaintiff shall not be entitled to costs unless the court is of opinion that there was reasonable ground for bringing the action,

(c) any tort-feasor liable in respect of that damage may recover contribution from any other tort-feasor who is, or would if sued have been, liable in respect of the same damage, whether as a joint tort-feasor or otherwise, so, however, that no person shall be entitled to recover contribution under this section from any person entitled to be indemnified by that person in respect of the liability in respect of which the contribution is sought.

(2) In any proceedings for contribution under this section the amount of the contribution recoverable from any person shall be such as may be found by the court to be just and equitable having regard to the extent of that person’s responsibility for the damage; and the court shall have power to exempt any person from liability to make contribution, or to direct that the contribution to be recovered from any person shall amount to a complete indemnity.

(3) For the purposes of this section:

(a) the expressions “parent” and “child” have the same meanings as they have for the purposes of the Compensation to Relatives Act of 1897 as amended by subsequent Acts, and

(b) the reference in this section to “the judgment first given” shall, in a case where that judgment is reversed on appeal, be construed as a reference to the judgment first given which is not so reversed and, in a case where a judgment is varied on appeal, be construed as a reference to that judgment as so varied, and

(c) the expression spouse of a person includes the de facto partner of a person at the time of his or her death.

(3A) For the purposes of this section, where a person commits a tort and the Crown is vicariously liable under section 8 of the Law Reform (Vicarious Liability) Act 1983 in respect of that tort, the Crown and the person are joint tort-feasors.

(4) Nothing in this section shall:

(a) apply with respect to any tort committed before the commencement of this Part, or

(a1) apply so as to cause the Crown and a person in the service of the Crown to be joint tort-feasors with respect to a tort to which section 8 of the Law Reform (Vicarious Liability) Act 1983 applies committed before the day appointed and notified under section 2 (2) of the Law Reform (Vicarious Liability) Act 1983, or

(b) affect any criminal proceedings against any person in respect of any wrongful act, or

(c) render enforceable any agreement for indemnity which would not have been enforceable if this section had not been passed.

(5) An amendment made to this section by the Miscellaneous Acts Amendment (Relationships) Act 2002 does not apply in respect of an action where the tort concerned occurred before the commencement of the amendment.

provisions.sourceLine: s 8  Definitions
provisions.oneLine: Section 8 defines the terms governing the contributory-negligence apportionment Part.
provisions.plain: These definitions govern Part 3. Claimant and contributory negligence refer to s 9(1); court means the court determining the claim, and damage includes death and personal injury. A wrong is either an act or omission creating tort liability for which common-law contributory negligence is available, or breach of a contractual care duty concurrent and co-extensive with a tort care duty. Not every tort or contractual breach meets that definition.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: A claimant pleads careless professional advice in contract. Compare the actual contractual care duty with the tort duty: the contractual route in the definition of wrong requires them to be concurrent and co-extensive. If the claim instead sounds in tort, ask whether contributory negligence is available at common law for that tort. The definition of damage expressly includes personal injury and loss of life.
conditions: Definitions apply in Part 3.
Claimant and contributory negligence: see s 9(1).
Court: the court by or before which the claim falls to be determined.
Damage includes loss of life and personal injury.
Wrong limb (a): an act or omission giving rise to tort liability for which contributory negligence is a common-law defence.
Wrong limb (b): breach of a contractual care duty concurrent and co-extensive with a tort care duty.
limits: The wrong definition is not every tort or every breach of contract.
Read with s 9 and any independently applicable CLA provisions.
provisions.examUse: Read the definitions before applying s 9.
pitfalls: Do not assume every contractual breach is a wrong under this Part.
provisions.text:
In this Part:

claimant—see section 9 (1).

contributory negligence—see section 9 (1).

court, in relation to any claim, means the court by or before which the claim falls to be determined.

damage includes loss of life and personal injury.

wrong means an act or omission that:

(a) gives rise to a liability in tort in respect of which a defence of contributory negligence is available at common law, or

(b) amounts to a breach of a contractual duty of care that is concurrent and co-extensive with a duty of care in tort.

provisions.sourceLine: s 9  Apportionment of liability in cases of contributory negligence
provisions.oneLine: Contributory negligence generally reduces damages by a just-and-equitable responsibility share, rather than defeating the claim.
provisions.plain: If damage is partly the claimant’s own failure of reasonable care and partly another person’s wrong, the claim is not defeated simply by the claimant’s contributory negligence. Damages are reduced by the extent the court finds just and equitable, having regard to the claimant’s share of responsibility. Contractual defences remain available, and an applicable contractual or statutory liability maximum still caps recovery. Read with the Part’s definitions and CLA ss 5R and 5S where applicable; s 5S permits a 100% reduction if just and equitable.
provisions.concreteExplanation: Illustrative hypothetical: Both a claimant and an adviser contribute to the same damage. The court reasons about responsibility before selecting a reduction; s 9 supplies no automatic percentage. A surviving contractual defence is not erased by the apportionment rule, and any applicable contractual or statutory maximum still limits the damages recoverable. In a negligence claim governed by CLA s 5S, a just and equitable reduction can reach 100%.
conditions: Damage results partly from the claimant’s failure to take reasonable care and partly from another person’s wrong as defined by s 8.
The reduction is what the court thinks just and equitable having regard to the claimant’s share in responsibility for the damage.
exceptions: Subsection (1) does not defeat any defence arising under a contract.
limits: An applicable contract or enactment limiting liability caps the amount recoverable under subsection (1) at that maximum.
Where applicable, CLA ss 5R and 5S must also be considered; s 5S permits a just and equitable 100% reduction.
provisions.examUse: Connect the apportionment rationale to the facts and the CLA provisions.
pitfalls: Do not claim that contributory negligence can never defeat a claim after CLA s 5S.
provisions.text:
(1) If a person (the claimant) suffers damage as the result partly of the claimant’s failure to take reasonable care (contributory negligence) and partly of the wrong of any other person:

(a) a claim in respect of the damage is not defeated by reason of the contributory negligence of the claimant, and

(b) the damages recoverable in respect of the wrong are to be reduced to such extent as the court thinks just and equitable having regard to the claimant’s share in the responsibility for the damage.

(2) Subsection (1) does not operate to defeat any defence arising under a contract.

(3) If any contract or enactment providing for the limitation of liability is applicable to the claim, the amount of damages recoverable by the claimant by virtue of subsection (1) is not to exceed the maximum limit so applicable.
